summary:
I developed Space Detectives: The Forgotten Explorers, an interactive learning website that helps school-age students discover the stories behind NASA equipment on the Moon, Mars and in deep space.

Students become space detectives. They meet Opportunity, the Apollo Moon reflectors, Ingenuity and Voyager, explore their parts, try simple science models, and use NASA evidence to explain what happened and what we learned. They can build their own Space Museum, create a comic or short story, and earn Space Coins to decorate a personal room.

My project addresses the challenge by connecting each machine to its purpose, science and mission status. Students discover that an ended mission can still be a success, while some equipment continues helping scientists.

I designed the activities especially for learners who find long texts and difficult English challenging. Short instructions, visual explanations, selected Bahasa Melayu support and optional narration make space science easier to approach. I want students to understand the science and feel ready to tell someone else about it.
details:
Space Detectives is a learning website for students around 10 to 15 years old. We wanted young learners to understand what NASA equipment actually did, how it worked and why its achievements still matter. Students investigate a question and then use what they learned to tell the explorer’s story.

How students use it

Meet. Students meet an explorer through a short story and find a useful part, such as a solar panel, rotor or antenna.

Try. They make a prediction and change something in a simple science model. They watch the result before deciding what it means.

Solve. They inspect a NASA record and put picture cards in order to explain the science. Feedback and hints help them try again.

Reveal. They discover what the equipment made possible, review a short quiz, and can build an exhibit by choosing supporting evidence and explaining the discovery.

Opportunity, Apollo and Ingenuity are the three core missions, each designed for about 10 minutes. Voyager is an optional bonus. Extra reading and discussion can take longer.

Explorer: Opportunity rover

What students try: Change the dust level and observe the model solar power.

What they learn: Connect sunlight to electrical energy, then examine separate rock images and mineral evidence about past water on Mars.

Explorer: Apollo Moon reflectors

What students try: Send a model light pulse and compare the round trip at two distances.

What they learn: Understand how returning light helps measure distance, and why a passive reflector can remain useful without a battery.

Explorer: Ingenuity helicopter

What students try: Compare two real flight records, then explore a model of gas and rotor lift on Earth and Mars.

What they learn: Understand the challenge of flight in thin air and the achievement of a technology demonstration that completed 72 flights.

Explorer: Voyager 1 and 2

What students try: Aim a model radio dish and send a measurement towards Earth.

What they learn: Connect science instruments to radio communication and learn how a mission can continue with a different purpose. This is the bonus mission.

Other ways to learn and share

My Space Museum. Students earn an exhibit by selecting the clues that support a claim and answering an explain-back question. For example, the Opportunity exhibit needs a rock image, a mineral measurement and geological context together.

My Stories. Seven guided fact cards help students create a six-panel comic, a short narrated story or a museum display. They can add their own words, preview the result, and print or download it. The animated story download can play offline; its NASA links still need internet.

Word help. Students tap a science word to see a short explanation and a visual sequence. Selected explanations include Bahasa Melayu support and a question to check understanding. Read-aloud is available when the browser supports it.

Solo or Buddy Expeditions. Students investigate alone or share one device with a friend or family member. They take turns predicting, testing and explaining, then make a small story from the evidence.

Space Coins and My Space Room. New learning tasks and reviewed quizzes earn virtual coins. Students spend them on decorations for a personal space room. There are no real-money purchases.

Ask Nova. An online AI science helper answers starter questions or a student’s own question in simple English. It receives checked mission facts and provides NASA source links. Students are reminded to check the answer with a teacher.

Teacher Guide. Teachers can choose activities by topic, time and class format. The guide includes short mission plans, a Word Lab, answer guides, group roles and a projector mode with larger text.

Optional Clue Quests. Extra tasks ask students to spot equipment in NASA images, arrange explanations and sort ideas. They give another way to practise using clues.

Tools and equipment

We developed the app with Lovable using React and TypeScript. TanStack Start and Router organise the pages and server functions. Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui and Radix UI support the interface. SVG and browser animation code power the science scenes. Vite supports the build.

The main learning activities run in a web browser. Progress and stories are stored on the same device, and students do not need an account. Ask Nova uses an online AI service through Lovable and the Vercel AI SDK. It is separate from the fixed answer checks in the learning activities.

A computer, tablet or phone with a suitable browser is enough to use the activities. A projector helps for whole-class teaching. A webcam is optional: Google MediaPipe lets a learner move an open hand to adjust the dust model. Camera frames are processed in the browser without recording or uploading them. Touch and mouse controls remain available.

What makes the project creative

The student becomes both an investigator and a storyteller. A mystery gives them a reason to look closely at the equipment. The experiment helps them understand an idea, while NASA records give them evidence about the real mission. Their museum exhibit or story then gives them a reason to explain it clearly to someone else.

The rewards connect to learning tasks, and the personal room gives students something of their own to build. The science words also open small visual explanations, so a student can get help at the point where a difficult word appears.

What we considered

We considered students’ reading confidence, especially learners using English as a second language. Most main tasks use taps and choices, with optional typing. Selected Bahasa Melayu guidance and read-aloud support make the activities easier to enter.

We also considered classroom use: short activities, one shared device for a pair, group roles, answer guides and a projector mode. Large controls, keyboard support and options to pause or step through animation help students work at their own pace.

Scientific accuracy shaped the activities. Real photographs, NASA illustrations, our learning models and imagined explorer voices are labelled separately. A model can help explain an idea, but it cannot replace a NASA measurement. Water evidence is not proof of life; one model laser trip cannot prove a change over decades; and radio waves are not sound.

Mission status also matters. Opportunity’s mission ended, Ingenuity’s flying ended, Apollo reflectors can still support research, and Voyager is presented using dated NASA status records. The app does not present these records as live telemetry.

Benefits and intended impact

We aim to help students explain the job of a piece of space equipment, connect an explanation to evidence and communicate a discovery in their own words. Teachers can use the same project for energy, light, flight, communication or science storytelling. Families can also join a Buddy Expedition.

Our intended impact is that students who might give up on a long science text can complete an investigation and feel ready to share what they understand. The app includes structured checks and quiz feedback to support this goal.
